passages.t: The families who went with Ezra
passages.happening:
Ezra now tells his own story. ‘These are the family heads and genealogical records of those who returned with me from Babylon during the reign of King Artaxerxes’ (verse 1).

First come two priestly families, the descendants of Phinehas and of Ithamar (verse 2). Then a descendant of King David: ‘from the descendants of David, Hattush of the descendants of Shecaniah’ (verse 3). Then twelve lay families, each with its leader and the number of men registered with him, from 28 men in one family to 300 in another (verses 3-14).
passages.hearers:
The list is shaped like the list of the first return in chapter 2: priests first, then the line of David, then the lay families with their numbers. After the priests and the son of David, twelve family groups are named, perhaps an echo of the twelve tribes.

The men listed number about 1,500. With women and children besides, the whole company may have numbered several thousand.

They set out in the first month of Artaxerxes' seventh year. On the traditional dating, that was the spring of 458 BC.

This is the second great return in the book, and it is told in the first person. The voice is Ezra's own, and he names the company family by family, as the book has done from the beginning.
passages.later: The family of David appears again in Chronicles, which traces David's line after the exile through Zerubbabel and names a Hattush among the descendants of Shecaniah: ‘Shemaiah and his sons: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat’ (1 Chronicles 3:22).
passages.asks: Each family on this list chose to leave Babylon for a small, poor province far away. Ask what it costs to leave a settled life for God's work in a harder place. And ask who would go with you, and with whom you would go.

passages.t: No Levites, and a fast by the canal
passages.happening:
‘Now I assembled these exiles at the canal that flows to Ahava, and we camped there three days. And when I searched among the people and priests, I found no Levites there’ (verse 15).

Ezra sends a group of leaders and teachers to Iddo, ‘the leader at Casiphia’ (verse 17), asking for ministers for the house of God. ‘And since the gracious hand of our God was upon us’ (verse 18), they bring back Sherebiah, a man of insight, with his sons and brothers, and Hashabiah and Jeshaiah with their families, thirty-eight Levites in all, and 220 temple servants, all of them named (verses 18-20).

Then Ezra calls a fast. ‘And there by the Ahava Canal I proclaimed a fast, so that we might humble ourselves before our God’ (verse 21), and ask him to keep them, their children and their goods safe on the road. ‘For I was ashamed to ask the king for an escort of soldiers and horsemen to protect us from our enemies on the road’ (verse 22), since they had told the king, “The hand of our God is gracious to all who seek Him, but His great anger is against all who forsake Him” (verse 22).

‘So we fasted and petitioned our God about this, and He granted our request’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The Ahava Canal was in Babylonia, but no one now knows exactly where. Casiphia is unknown too. The way Ezra describes it has led some scholars to suggest that it was a center of Jewish religious life in the exile, perhaps even a place of worship, but the text does not say so.

The missing Levites are no surprise to a reader of chapter 2, where only seventy-four came home with the first return. Ezra will not go without them. A temple needs its servants.

Travel between Babylonia and Judah meant months on roads where bandits preyed on caravans, and a company carrying gold and silver was an obvious target. Royal envoys normally traveled with soldiers. Ezra's refusal was a matter of consistency, not a rule against escorts. He had told the king that God's hand protects those who seek him, and he felt that asking for soldiers would contradict his own witness.

So he fasts. In the ancient world, fasting was a way of humbling oneself before God, often with prayer, in times of danger or grief. The verb for humble here is the one the law uses for the Day of Atonement. A fast was not a way of forcing God's hand. It was a way of saying, with the whole body, that everything depended on him.
passages.later:
The law of the Day of Atonement uses the same word: ‘On the tenth day of the seventh month, you shall humble yourselves and not do any work’ (Leviticus 16:29).

Years later, Nehemiah traveled with soldiers: ‘The king had also sent army officers and cavalry with me’ (Nehemiah 2:9).
passages.hard:
Was Ezra right to go without soldiers, when Nehemiah later took them?

Ezra's choice was a matter of consistency, not a rule. He had told the king that God's hand protects those who seek him, and he felt that asking for soldiers would undercut what he had said. Nehemiah, sent as governor with the king's letters, accepted army officers and cavalry, and the book does not fault him for it.

The two men did not hold different beliefs about God's protection. They faced different situations and answered them in different ways. Ezra's fast does not teach that trusting God means refusing ordinary protection. Nehemiah himself prayed and posted a guard.
passages.asks: Ezra was ashamed to ask for what his own words said he did not need. Ask whether your actions match what you have said about God. And ask what you do with fear: whether you bring it to God in prayer before you set out, as this company did.

passages.t: The treasure weighed, and the arrival
passages.happening:
Ezra sets apart twelve of the leading priests, with Sherebiah, Hashabiah and ten of their brothers (verse 24), and weighs out to them the silver and gold and the articles that the king, his counselors, his leaders and all the Israelites there had given for the house of God (verse 25). It is a great treasure: hundreds of talents of silver, a hundred talents of gold, twenty gold bowls, and two articles of fine polished bronze, ‘as precious as gold’ (verse 27).

Then he tells them, “You are holy to the LORD, and these articles are holy. The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the LORD, the God of your fathers” (verse 28). “Guard them carefully until you weigh them out in the chambers of the house of the LORD in Jerusalem” (verse 29).

‘On the twelfth day of the first month we set out from the Ahava Canal to go to Jerusalem, and the hand of our God was upon us to protect us from the hands of the enemies and bandits along the way’ (verse 31). They arrive and rest for three days. On the fourth day the treasure is weighed out in the house of God into the hands of Meremoth the priest and those with him. ‘Everything was verified by number and weight, and the total weight was recorded at that time’ (verse 34).

The returned exiles offer burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering (verse 35). And they deliver the king's orders to the royal satraps and governors west of the Euphrates, ‘who proceeded to assist the people and the house of God’ (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
The weighing shows both ancient practice and Ezra's honesty. Coins were still fairly new, and much wealth was measured by weight. By weighing the treasure out to named priests and Levites in Babylon, and having it weighed again and written down in Jerusalem, Ezra made sure that no one could accuse him or them of theft. The verb to weigh comes four times in the chapter.

He also treats the treasure as sacred. Something holy is set apart for God and belongs to him. The people set apart for God carry what has been set apart for him.

The arrival mirrors the departure: three days of rest in Jerusalem, as there had been three days of camping at Ahava. And the sacrifices are for all Israel: twelve bulls, twelve goats, and ninety-six rams, which is eight times twelve. The company, mostly from Judah and Benjamin, offers for the whole people.

The satraps were the governors of the great Persian provinces. With the king's orders delivered, Ezra's commission had the force of law in the region.
passages.later: Paul took the same kind of care when he carried the churches' gift to Jerusalem: ‘We hope to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift’ (2 Corinthians 8:20).
passages.hard:
How much was the treasure?

The amounts in verses 26 and 27 are enormous. The 650 talents of silver alone would be over twenty tons, by the usual estimate of a talent.

Some scholars think the figures grew in copying, or that a lighter talent was used. Others take them as they stand, since the gifts came from the king, his counselors and the whole Jewish community of Babylonia. On any reading, the point of the passage is not the size of the gift but its safe and honest delivery.
passages.asks: Ezra had the treasure weighed twice and the weight written down. Ask how open you are about money that others have trusted to you. And ask what it would mean to treat what belongs to God, and to other people, as holy.
